entries.title: Less-Is-Better Effect – when less looks better because the comparison is missing
entries.description:
The less-is-better effect appears when we evaluate a smaller or objectively lower-value option more positively because an easier contextual cue makes it look better, especially when options are judged separately. More can lose to less because context has a surprisingly good marketing department.

Classic examples
- Gifts – in the original research, a $45 scarf could make the giver seem more generous than a $55 coat when each gift was judged separately. The scarf looked expensive for a scarf; the coat looked modest for a coat.
- Ice cream – people could value a smaller but overfilled serving more than a larger but underfilled serving. Fullness was easier to judge than the exact amount of ice cream.
- Product sets – a smaller set containing only intact items could be valued more than a larger set that contained more intact items overall but also some broken pieces.

A better check
- Compare serious options side by side when separate evaluation may hide the total difference.
- Separate total value from the easiest visible cue: fullness, percentage intact, category price, or another local reference point.
- Ask what changed in absolute terms. Did we really get less value, or did the larger option simply look worse against its container or category?
- Count real costs too. Extra broken items can create disposal or effort costs, so 'more' is not automatically better outside the experimental setup.

The effect is not a rule that smaller options are secretly superior. It is a warning that when comparison is difficult, we may judge the easiest reference point instead of the thing we actually care about.
